hints: Focus on what atoms are added in each reaction and whether the product carbons end up with four different groups.
Draw X as 1,2-dibromo-1-methylcyclohexane and check C1 and C2 for chirality, then draw Y as 1-bromo-1-methylcyclohexane and check C1.
Remember Br2 adds anti via a bromonium ion that can form on either face and open at either carbon, while a tertiary bromoalkane carbon with two identical ring paths cannot be a chiral centre.
walkthrough:
**Identify products X and Y**

Think first about connectivity, not 3D shape. Addition to the double bond gives saturated products.

$$\text{1-methylcyclohexene} + \text{Br}_2 \rightarrow \text{1,2-dibromo-1-methylcyclohexane (X)}$$
$$\text{1-methylcyclohexene} + \text{HBr} \rightarrow \text{1-bromo-1-methylcyclohexane (Y, Markovnikov)}$$

**Check Y for chiral centres**

Y has Br and $\text{CH}_3$ both on C1. That carbon is joined to C2 and C6 of the ring.

Going clockwise C1-C2-C3-C4 and anticlockwise C1-C6-C5-C4 are identical $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2$ paths, so C1 has two identical groups and is not chiral. No other carbons in Y have Br or changed groups, so Y has no stereoisomers.

**Check X for chiral centres**

X has Br on C1 which also has $\text{CH}_3$, and Br on C2 which also has H. C1 is joined to $\text{C(Br)HCH}_2$ on one side and $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2$ on the other, so its four groups are different.

Similarly C2 is joined to $\text{C(Br)(CH}_3\text{)CH}_2$ on one side and $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2$ on the other, so it is also chiral. Two chiral centres means up to $2^2 = 4$ stereoisomers.

**Decide if all four forms of X actually form**

Bromination goes through a cyclic bromonium ion by anti addition. The $\text{Br}^+$ can add to the top face or the bottom face of the flat alkene.

Each bromonium ion can then be opened by $\text{Br}^-$ at C1 or at C2 from the back side. That gives two different relative arrangements of $\text{CH}_3$ and Br for each face, so four stereoisomers in total as two pairs of enantiomers.

options.A: This undercounts X. It is tempting to think only trans addition gives one pair of enantiomers, but opening of the bromonium ion at C1 versus C2 gives a second diastereomer, so X has four, not two, stereoisomers.
options.B: This is wrong on both sides. X has four stereoisomers, not two, and Y has no chiral centre because C1 carries two identical ring segments, so it cannot have four stereoisomers.
options.C: Correct. X is 1,2-dibromo-1-methylcyclohexane with two chiral centres at C1 and C2, formed as four stereoisomers via top and bottom bromonium ions opened at either carbon. Y is 1-bromo-1-methylcyclohexane where C1 has Me, Br and two identical CH2 ring paths, so it is achiral and has no stereoisomers.
options.D: X is correctly given as four stereoisomers, but Y is incorrectly given as chiral. Students sometimes think the tertiary bromide carbon is chiral because it has Me and Br, forgetting the symmetry of the cyclohexane ring makes the two sides identical.
